source: ACIAR AH/2005/086 'Smallholder Cattle Best Practice Manual' (Windsor, Bush & Young), Best Practice Health and Husbandry of Cattle, Cambodia -- hosted at mekonglivestock.wordpress.com (University of Sydney / GDAHP project site)
text: Blackleg is a bacterial disease most often affecting young, well-fed cattle; the bacteria live in cattle intestines, are shed onto soil, and other animals may ingest them while grazing -- it does not spread directly from animal to animal by contact. Multiple cattle in a herd can be affected in an outbreak. Signs include lameness, rapid breathing, depression, fever, and hot, painful, spongy swelling of the hip, shoulder, or chest; affected animals usually die within 12-48 hours. Treatment with antibiotics is rarely successful, so prevention is the priority: vaccinate calves twice at 2-6 months of age, and in high-risk areas revaccinate at 1 and 5 years; in an outbreak, all susceptible cattle can be vaccinated and given prophylactic penicillin.
